_comment: Facts the manuscript states in prose but that the site needs as structured data. Nothing here is invented: every value traces to a claim in resources/manuscript/full-document.md. Where the manuscript is silent about a state, the field is omitted and the site says so rather than guessing. homeFeatured names the worked examples the front page shows; build-content.mjs lifts their text into site.json so the home page needs no chapter prose.

timeline.title: Section 529 is created
timeline.body: The Small Business Job Protection Act, signed 20 August 1996, gives states authority to establish Qualified Tuition Programs. Utah is among the first to launch, under its Utah Educational Savings Plan.

timeline.title: Withdrawals become tax-free
timeline.body: EGTRRA exempts qualified higher-education distributions from federal income tax entirely — the change that turned an imperfect savings tool into one of the most powerful tax-advantaged vehicles available. The provisions were scheduled to expire in 2010.

timeline.title: Made permanent
timeline.body: The Pension Protection Act locks in what EGTRRA created, removing the sunset. Families could finally plan knowing the rules would not shift.

timeline.title: Technology qualifies
timeline.body: The American Taxpayer Relief Act acknowledges that laptops, tablets, and internet service are academic necessities rather than luxuries.

timeline.title: Refunds can be recontributed
timeline.body: The PATH Act lets an account holder return a refunded tuition payment to the 529 within 60 days without penalty.

timeline.title: K–12 tuition qualifies
timeline.body: The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act allows up to $10,000 per beneficiary per year for elementary and secondary tuition — public, private, or religious. Thirty-seven states and D.C. adopt conforming rules; a handful decline.

timeline.title: Apprenticeships and student loans
timeline.body: The SECURE Act adds registered apprenticeship programs certified by the Department of Labor, plus $10,000 in lifetime distributions to repay the beneficiary's student loans.

timeline.title: SECURE 2.0 answers over-funding
timeline.body: Enacted in the final days of December 2022 and effective 2024: unused 529 assets may be rolled into a Roth IRA in the beneficiary's name, converting a potential liability into a retirement asset.

timeline.title: Tutors, credentials, and ABLE
timeline.body: H.R. 1 — the One Big Beautiful Bill — doubles the K–12 cap to $20,000 and broadens it beyond tuition to tutors, curriculum materials and standardized test fees. It extends eligibility to vocational and professional credential programs, and removes the expiry on 529-to-ABLE rollovers.

timeline.title: Thirty years on
timeline.body: Thirty years in, some 17.7 million accounts hold around $603 billion across 90 plans. Around 500 institutions outside the United States accept 529 funding. Half of families now save with one — and parent awareness remains the biggest growth opportunity.

comparison.footnote: The 530A account offers one genuine perk: a $1,000 government seed deposit for children born between 2025 and 2028, plus possible philanthropic or employer contributions. The two are not mutually exclusive. But as an education savings vehicle the 530A falls short on every major tax dimension.

anyPlanDeduction.label: Tax benefit for contributions to any state's plan
anyPlanDeduction.detail: Nine states extend state tax benefits to contributions made to any 529 plan, not just their own — letting residents chase the best plan nationally without giving up the break. Thirty-seven states and D.C. offer a contribution deduction or credit at all.

credit.label: Offer a tax credit rather than a deduction
credit.detail: A credit reduces your tax bill dollar-for-dollar rather than reducing taxable income, which usually makes it the better of the two. Four plans provide a credit instead of a deduction — Indiana, Oregon, Utah and Vermont — while Minnesota lets you choose between the two.

noDeduction.label: No state tax deduction for contributions
noDeduction.detail: In states with no deduction, shopping nationally for the best plan — lowest fees, preferred allocation options — is suggested.

k12NotAllowed.label: Do not allow K–12 qualified distributions
k12NotAllowed.detail: A withdrawal for K–12 may be tax-free federally but taxable at the state level in these jurisdictions. California further penalizes such withdrawals by an extra 2.5%.

morningstarGold.label: Morningstar Gold rated, November 2025
morningstarGold.detail: Morningstar's 529 ratings, released in November 2025, gave Gold to these five plans for their investment option design and low fees. Plans elsewhere carry higher expense ratios that erode returns over eighteen years.

chapterBlurbs.forward: Six things most families get wrong about 529 accounts — starting with the fact that the money never stops being yours.
chapterBlurbs.federal-tips: The whole federal framework in one place: control, deposits, taxes, K–12, college, life after graduation, and estate planning.
chapterBlurbs.history: How a state-capital experiment became federal law in 1996, and the eight expansions that followed it.
chapterBlurbs.state-differences: Every state but Wyoming runs its own plan with its own rules. What actually varies, and what to check before choosing one.
chapterBlurbs.basics: Owner, beneficiary, successor — who controls the money, how to change any of it without a fee, how to roll it to another state, and every route for getting money in.
chapterBlurbs.taxes: Deduction or credit, tax-free growth, contribution ceilings and deadlines, and exactly what a non-qualified withdrawal costs you.
chapterBlurbs.fund-selection: What you need to open an account, target-date against static allocations, the two-changes-a-year rule, the real risk of loss, and why starting early beats timing the market.
chapterBlurbs.k-12: Private tuition, curriculum and software, tutors, therapies and test fees — plus the thirteen states that don't allow any of it.
chapterBlurbs.post-secondary: Qualified schools, room and board, computers, apprenticeships, credentials and scholarships — and how a 529 affects financial aid.
chapterBlurbs.after-graduation: Student loans, transfers down the family, the Roth rollover, and paying for licensing and continuing education across a whole career.
chapterBlurbs.estate-planning: Completed gifts, superfunding, generation-skipping transfer tax, bankruptcy protection, and moving wealth across generations.
chapterBlurbs.maximizing: Five advanced playbooks — funding, K–12, post-secondary, after graduation, and estate planning.
chapterBlurbs.comparisons: Head to head against prepaid tuition plans, Coverdell ESAs, UGMA/UTMA custodial accounts, a child Roth IRA, and the new 530A “Trump account”.
